modern: Do you not see how craftsmen accommodate themselves up to a point to those who are not skilled in their craft—but nevertheless they hold on to the principles of their art, and will not bear to depart from them? Is it not strange if the architect and the physician have more respect for the principles of their own arts than man has for his own reason, which he shares with the gods?
original: Dost thou not see how the handicrafts-men accommodate themselves up to a certain point to those who are not skilled in their craft—nevertheless they cling to the reason [the principles] of their art, and do not endure to depart from it? Is it not strange if the architect and the physician shall have more respect to the reason [the principles] of their own arts than man to his own reason, which is common to him and the gods?

explained.summary: Skilled craftspeople will go along with untrained clients up to a point, but they won’t abandon the core principles of their trade. Architects and doctors stick to their rules. So isn’t it strange if a person has less respect for their own reason, the thing they share with the gods, than a builder has for building?
explained.today: A good plumber will listen to what you want but won’t fit the pipe in a way that will leak. Yet people will drop their own principles to please the room in a meeting or keep the peace at dinner. Your reason deserves at least as much loyalty as a tradesperson’s standards.
